rows.stem: In the circuit shown, the charge on the left plate of 20 \(\mu\mathrm{F}\) capacitor is \(-\,50\) \(\mu\mathrm{C}\). The charge on the right plate of the 12 \(\mu\mathrm{F}\) capacitor is :
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED — the stem names only two of the four capacitors and says nothing about how any of them are connected; the network exists only in the drawing. What is drawn: a horizontal two-terminal chain between an open circle on the left and an open circle on the right. From the left terminal a capacitor labelled \(20\,\mu\mathrm{F}\) leads to a junction, from which the wire splits into two parallel branches that rejoin at a second junction — the upper branch carries a capacitor labelled \(12\,\mu\mathrm{F}\) and the lower branch one labelled \(8\,\mu\mathrm{F}\). From the second junction a capacitor labelled \(4\,\mu\mathrm{F}\) leads to the right terminal. Every capacitor is drawn as the standard two-parallel-plate symbol and no plate is individually marked, so the 'left plate' / 'right plate' language of the stem refers to orientation on the page. Page idx 4.
rows.solution:
**The answer is (C): \(30\ \mu\)C.**

**Read the network.** The \(20\ \mu\)F, the parallel pair \(\left(12\ \mu\mathrm{F}\ \| \ 8\ \mu\mathrm{F}\right)\) and the \(4\ \mu\)F are all **in series** between the two terminals.

**Step 1 — the charge on the series chain.** In a series combination every element carries the **same magnitude** of charge. The \(20\ \mu\)F's left plate holds \(-50\ \mu\)C, so its right plate holds \(+50\ \mu\)C, and \(50\ \mu\)C is the charge flowing through the whole chain.

**Step 2 — how it divides between the parallel branches.** The \(12\) and the \(8\) share the **same potential difference**, so the charge splits in proportion to capacitance:

\(q_{12} = 50 \times \dfrac{12}{12 + 8} = 50 \times \dfrac{12}{20} = 30\ \mu\mathrm{C}\)

\(q_8 = 50 \times \dfrac{8}{20} = 20\ \mu\mathrm{C}\)

*(A check: the pair combines to \(12 + 8 = 20\ \mu\)F, matching the \(20\ \mu\)F beside it — which is why they carry the same total charge.)*

**Step 3 — the SIGN on the right plate.** Trace the plates along the chain. The middle conductor — the \(20\ \mu\)F's right plate together with the **left** plates of the \(12\) and the \(8\) — is isolated and was neutral, so its total charge stays zero:

\(\left(+50\right) + q_{\text{left}}^{12} + q_{\text{left}}^{8} = 0\)

giving \(q_{\text{left}}^{12} = -30\ \mu\)C and \(q_{\text{left}}^{8} = -20\ \mu\)C. Each capacitor's two plates carry equal and opposite charges, so the \(12\ \mu\)F's **right** plate holds

\(\boxed{\ +30\ \mu\mathrm{C}\ }\)

**The sign is half the question**, which is why both \(+30\) and \(-30\) are offered. Working plate by plate along the chain — and using the fact that each isolated internal conductor stays neutral — is what fixes it; guessing from the \(-50\) alone does not.

**Why charge divides in PROPORTION to capacitance in parallel but is EQUAL in series.** Parallel elements share a voltage, and \(q = CV\) then makes \(q \propto C\). Series elements are linked by isolated conductors that must stay neutral, which forces the same \(q\) through each regardless of its capacitance.

**Note that the \(4\ \mu\)F never entered the calculation.** It carries the same \(50\ \mu\)C as everything else in the chain, but its value is irrelevant to the split between the \(12\) and the \(8\). Only the ratio \(12 : 8\) matters.

rows.stem: A steady current I is passed through a conductor at room temperature for time t. It is observed that its temperature rises by \(0{\cdot}5^{\circ}\)C. If 2I current is passed through the conductor (at room temperature) for the same duration, the rise in its temperature will be approximately :
rows.solution:
**The answer is (C): \(2{\cdot}0\ ^\circ\)C.**

**Joule heating.** The heat produced in a conductor in time \(t\) is

\(H = I^{2}Rt\)

**and that heat raises the temperature:**

\(H = mc\,\Delta T \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \Delta T = \dfrac{I^{2}Rt}{mc}\)

**Everything except \(I\) is unchanged** — the same conductor \(\left(R, m, c\right)\), the same duration \(t\), and the same starting temperature. So

\(\Delta T \propto I^{2}\)

**Doubling the current.**

\(\dfrac{\Delta T_2}{\Delta T_1} = \left(\dfrac{2I}{I}\right)^{2} = 4\)

\(\boxed{\ \Delta T_2 = 4 \times 0{\cdot}5 = 2{\cdot}0\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}\ }\)

**The SQUARE is the whole question**, and option (A), \(1{\cdot}0\ ^\circ\)C, is there for anyone who takes the rise as simply proportional to the current. Heat depends on \(I^{2}\), so doubling the current **quadruples** it.

**Why "approximately" appears in the stem.** \(R\) is treated as constant, but a conductor's resistance **rises** with temperature. The hotter run of the second case therefore has a slightly larger \(R\) throughout, producing a little more heat than the simple \(I^{2}\) scaling predicts. The effect is small over a rise of a couple of degrees — for copper, \(\alpha \approx 4 \times 10^{-3}\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}^{-1}\), so \(2\ ^\circ\)C changes \(R\) by under \(1\%\) — but it is real, and the word acknowledges it.

**It also acknowledges the second idealisation**: that all the heat stays in the conductor. In reality some is lost to the surroundings, and the loss grows with temperature, pulling the other way. Both corrections are small here.

**The same \(I^{2}\) dependence elsewhere.** It is why transmission lines carry power at **high voltage and low current** — halving the current cuts the line losses to a quarter — and why a fuse of twice the rating dissipates four times the heat at its limit.

**A check on the options.** \(4{\cdot}0\ ^\circ\)C would be the answer if \(\Delta T\) went as \(I^{2}\) **and** the starting rise were \(1\ ^\circ\)C, or as \(I^{3}\) from \(0{\cdot}5\); \(1{\cdot}5\ ^\circ\)C corresponds to no clean power at all. Only the factor of **four** applied to \(0{\cdot}5\) gives a listed value.

rows.subtopic: Bohr Model of the Hydrogen Atom
rows.stem: The minimum energy required to free the electron from the ground state of the hydrogen atom is :
rows.solution:
**The answer is (C): \(13{\cdot}6\) eV.**

**The ground state of hydrogen.**

\(E_n = -\dfrac{13{\cdot}6}{n^{2}}\ \mathrm{eV} \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad E_1 = -13{\cdot}6\ \mathrm{eV}\)

**To free the electron** means to carry it to \(n = \infty\), where the energy is zero and the electron is no longer bound. The energy required is the difference:

\(\Delta E = E_\infty - E_1 = 0 - \left(-13{\cdot}6\right)\)

\(\boxed{\ \Delta E = 13{\cdot}6\ \mathrm{eV}\ }\)

**This is the IONISATION ENERGY of hydrogen**, and it is exactly the magnitude of the ground-state energy. The minus sign in \(E_1\) says the electron is bound by \(13{\cdot}6\) eV; removing it costs precisely that much.

**Why the energies are negative at all.** The zero of energy is taken at infinite separation, with the electron at rest. Any bound state must lie **below** that, so every \(E_n\) is negative — and the deeper the level, the more tightly the electron is held.

**Option (A), \(3{\cdot}4\) eV, is the FIRST EXCITED state's binding**, \(\left|E_2\right|\). It is the energy needed to free an electron already in \(n = 2\) — a different question, and a smaller answer, since that electron starts four times further out and much less tightly held.

**Option (D) is the trap for a half-remembered fact.** \(13{\cdot}6 - 3{\cdot}4 = 10{\cdot}2\) eV **is** a real and important number — the energy of the \(1 \to 2\) transition, the first line of the Lyman series — but it merely **excites** the atom, lifting the electron to \(n = 2\). It does not free it. Freeing requires the full \(13{\cdot}6\) eV.

**The distinction the question is testing.** **Excitation** moves the electron to a higher bound level; **ionisation** removes it altogether. The excitation energies for hydrogen are \(10{\cdot}2\), \(12{\cdot}1\), \(12{\cdot}75\) eV and so on, creeping up towards — but never reaching — the ionisation energy of \(13{\cdot}6\) eV. That the levels crowd together like this is the \(1/n^{2}\) dependence at work.

**A note on what happens above \(13{\cdot}6\) eV.** A photon of exactly \(13{\cdot}6\) eV frees the electron with zero kinetic energy; anything more and the surplus appears as kinetic energy of the freed electron. That is the photoelectric equation applied to an atom, with \(13{\cdot}6\) eV playing the part of the work function.

rows.stem: Calculate the value of the current passing through the battery in the given circuit diagram.
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED — the stem names no component and no value at all; the entire circuit exists only in the drawing. What is drawn: a closed loop containing a battery labelled \(6\,\mathrm{V}\) along the bottom rail. Above it runs a chain of four labelled points. From the left rail a resistor labelled \(10\,\Omega\) leads from a point marked A to a point marked B; from B a resistor labelled \(5\,\Omega\) leads to a point marked C; from C a resistor labelled \(40\,\Omega\) leads to a point marked D on the right rail. A further resistor labelled \(20\,\Omega\) is drawn as an arc ABOVE that chain, and a second resistor labelled \(20\,\Omega\) is drawn as an arc BELOW it. Which pair of lettered points each of those two \(20\,\Omega\) arcs bridges is exactly what decides the answer and is legible only in the drawing, so it is withheld here. Page idx 10.
rows.solution:
**Recognise the shape first.** Nodes \(A\) and \(D\) are the battery terminals, \(B\) and \(C\) are the other two junctions, and the \(5\ \Omega\) between \(B\) and \(C\) is the **bridge**. The four arms are

\(R_{AB} = 10\ \Omega, \quad R_{BD} = 20\ \Omega, \quad R_{AC} = 20\ \Omega, \quad R_{CD} = 40\ \Omega\)

**This is a WHEATSTONE BRIDGE, and it is balanced.**

\(\dfrac{R_{AB}}{R_{BD}} = \dfrac{10}{20} = \dfrac{1}{2} \qquad\text{and}\qquad \dfrac{R_{AC}}{R_{CD}} = \dfrac{20}{40} = \dfrac{1}{2}\)

The two ratios match, so \(V_B = V_C\) and **no current flows through the \(5\ \Omega\)**. It can simply be deleted from the circuit.

**Testing for balance BEFORE combining anything is the whole method here.** A bridge is not reducible by series-and-parallel rules in general — an unbalanced one needs Kirchhoff's equations or a star-delta transformation. Checking the ratio first is what turns this into a two-line problem.

**With the bridge removed, two simple series paths remain.**

\(A \to B \to D: \quad 10 + 20 = 30\ \Omega\)

\(A \to C \to D: \quad 20 + 40 = 60\ \Omega\)

**These are in parallel** between the battery terminals:

\(R_{eq} = \dfrac{30 \times 60}{30 + 60} = \dfrac{1800}{90} = 20\ \Omega\)

**The current through the battery.**

\(I = \dfrac{V}{R_{eq}} = \dfrac{6}{20}\)

\(\boxed{\ I = 0{\cdot}3\ \mathrm{A} = \dfrac{3}{10}\ \mathrm{A}\ }\)

**How the current splits.** The \(30\ \Omega\) branch takes \(6/30 = 0{\cdot}2\) A and the \(60\ \Omega\) branch \(6/60 = 0{\cdot}1\) A — together the \(0{\cdot}3\) A drawn from the battery \(\checkmark\). Twice as much goes through the branch of half the resistance, as it must.

**A check that the bridge really is balanced.** \(V_B\) is \(A\)'s potential less \(0{\cdot}2 \times 10 = 2\) V; \(V_C\) is \(A\)'s potential less \(0{\cdot}1 \times 20 = 2\) V. Equal, so nothing crosses the \(5\ \Omega\) \(\checkmark\).

**Note that the \(5\ \Omega\) is irrelevant WHATEVER its value.** Replace it with \(1\ \Omega\) or \(1000\ \Omega\) and the answer is unchanged, because no current flows through it either way. That insensitivity is exactly what makes a balanced bridge useful for measurement: the null reading does not depend on the galvanometer's own resistance.

rows.stem: In a Young's double-slit experiment, the intensity at the central maximum in the interference pattern on the screen is \(\mathrm{I_0}\). Find the intensity at a point on the screen where the path difference between the interfering waves is \(\dfrac{\lambda}{6}\).
rows.solution:
**Convert the path difference into a phase difference.**

\(\phi = \dfrac{2\pi}{\lambda}\times\Delta x = \dfrac{2\pi}{\lambda}\times\dfrac{\lambda}{6} = \dfrac{\pi}{3}\)

**The intensity distribution**, written in terms of the **central maximum** \(I_0\):

\(I = I_0\cos^{2}\left(\dfrac{\phi}{2}\right)\)

**Substituting.**

\(I = I_0\cos^{2}\left(\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right) = I_0\left(\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)^{2}\)

\(\boxed{\ I = \dfrac{3I_0}{4}\ }\)

**The HALF-ANGLE is where marks are lost.** The formula carries \(\cos^{2}\left(\phi/2\right)\), not \(\cos^{2}\phi\). Here \(\phi = \pi/3\), so the argument is \(\pi/6\) and \(\cos\left(\pi/6\right) = \sqrt{3}/2\). Using \(\cos^{2}\left(\pi/3\right) = 1/4\) instead would give \(I_0/4\) — a factor of three out.

**The same answer the long way**, which is worth seeing once:

\(I = I_1 + I_2 + 2\sqrt{I_1I_2}\cos\phi\)

With equal sources \(I_1 = I_2 = I\) and \(I_0 = 4I\) at the centre:

\(I' = I + I + 2I\cos\dfrac{\pi}{3} = 2I + 2I\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right) = 3I = \dfrac{3I_0}{4}\ \checkmark\)

**Note that \(I_0 = 4I\), not \(2I\).** At the central maximum the two waves are in phase, so the **amplitudes** add and the intensity is \(\left(a + a\right)^{2} = 4a^{2}\) — **four** times one beam alone, not twice. Energy is not created: the surplus at the maxima is exactly the deficit at the minima, and the average across the screen remains \(2I\).

**Reading the answer.** At \(\Delta x = \lambda/6\) the point is one-sixth of the way to the next bright fringe, and the intensity has already fallen to \(75\%\) of the peak. The pattern is broad rather than sharp — for two-slit interference the intensity varies smoothly as \(\cos^{2}\), unlike the tight peaks of a diffraction grating.

**Two checks at the extremes.** \(\Delta x = 0\) gives \(\cos^{2}0 = 1\) and \(I = I_0\) — the central maximum. \(\Delta x = \lambda/2\) gives \(\phi = \pi\), \(\cos^{2}\left(\pi/2\right) = 0\) and \(I = 0\) — a dark fringe. Both come out right, which is the quickest way to confirm the half-angle is in the right place.

rows.stem: Define the 'distance of closest approach'. An \(\alpha\)-particle of kinetic energy K is bombarded on a thin gold foil. Derive an expression for the 'distance of closest approach'.
rows.solution:
**Definition.**

The **distance of closest approach** is the minimum distance from the nucleus to which an alpha particle, projected directly at it, can get — the point at which it comes momentarily to rest and turns back.

Equivalently: it is the distance at which the alpha particle's **entire initial kinetic energy** has been converted into **electrostatic potential energy** of the alpha-nucleus system.

**The derivation.**

**Step 1 — the charges involved.** An alpha particle is a helium nucleus, carrying charge \(+2e\). The gold nucleus carries \(+Ze\), with \(Z = 79\).

**Step 2 — the energy balance at the turning point.** As the alpha approaches, the Coulomb repulsion does negative work on it and it slows. At the distance of closest approach \(d\) its speed is **zero**, so all of its kinetic energy \(K\) has become potential energy:

\(K = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\cdot\dfrac{\left(2e\right)\left(Ze\right)}{d}\)

**Step 3 — rearrange.**

\(\boxed{\ d = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\cdot\dfrac{2Ze^{2}}{K} = \dfrac{2Ze^{2}}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 K}\ }\)

**The factor of 2 is the alpha's own charge**, and omitting it is the standard slip — the expression is not \(Ze^{2}\) but \(2Ze^{2}\), because the projectile carries two elementary charges, not one.

**Reading the result.** \(d\) is **inversely** proportional to the kinetic energy: a faster alpha penetrates closer. And it is **directly** proportional to \(Z\), so a heavier target repels the alpha from further out. Neither the alpha's **mass** nor its speed appears explicitly — the whole argument is an energy balance from start to finish.

**A numerical feel.** For \(K = 5{\cdot}5\) MeV, typical of a natural alpha source, and gold's \(Z = 79\):

\(d = \dfrac{9 \times 10^{9} \times 2 \times 79 \times 1{\cdot}6 \times 10^{-19}}{5{\cdot}5 \times 10^{6}} \approx 4{\cdot}1 \times 10^{-14}\ \mathrm{m}\)

about **six times** the radius of a gold nucleus \(\left(\approx 7\ \mathrm{fm}\right)\).

**Why that matters for Rutherford's analysis.** The alpha is turned back well **outside** the nuclear surface, so only the **Coulomb** force acts throughout — the short-ranged strong nuclear force never comes into play. That is precisely why a scattering formula built from Coulomb's law alone described the data so well, and why \(d\) sets an **upper limit** on the nuclear radius. Firing harder eventually closes the gap, and the departure from the formula is historically how nuclear sizes were first measured.

**Why "head-on" is essential to the derivation.** A head-on approach has zero impact parameter, so the alpha's **whole** kinetic energy is available to be spent against the repulsion. A glancing approach keeps some kinetic energy at its turning point and comes no nearer than a larger distance.

rows.stem:
An electric field \(\vec{E}\) given by :
\(\vec{E} = 100\,\hat{i}\ \dfrac{\mathrm{N}}{\mathrm{C}}\) for x > 0
\(= -\,100\,\hat{i}\ \dfrac{\mathrm{N}}{\mathrm{C}}\) for x < 0
exists in a region. A right circular cylinder of length 10 cm and radius 2 cm, is placed in the region such that its axis coincides with x-axis and its two faces are at x = \(-\) 5 cm and x = 5 cm. Calculate :
(a) the net outward flux through the cylinder, and
(b) the net charge inside the cylinder.
rows.solution:
**The geometry.** A cylinder of radius \(r = 2\) cm and length \(10\) cm lies along the \(x\)-axis with its flat faces at \(x = -5\) cm and \(x = +5\) cm. The field points **away from the origin on both sides**: along \(+\hat{i}\) for \(x > 0\) and along \(-\hat{i}\) for \(x < 0\).

**The area of each flat face.**

\(A = \pi r^{2} = \pi\left(2 \times 10^{-2}\right)^{2} = 4\pi \times 10^{-4}\ \mathrm{m^{2}}\)

**(a) The net outward flux.**

**The CURVED surface contributes NOTHING.** Its outward normal points radially, perpendicular to the \(x\)-axis, while \(\vec{E}\) lies entirely along \(x\). So \(\vec{E}\cdot d\vec{S} = 0\) at every point of it.

**The RIGHT face**, at \(x = +5\) cm. Its outward normal is \(+\hat{i}\), and there \(\vec{E} = +100\,\hat{i}\):

\(\phi_R = \left(100\,\hat{i}\right)\cdot\left(A\,\hat{i}\right) = 100A = 100 \times 4\pi \times 10^{-4} = 4\pi \times 10^{-2}\ \mathrm{N\,m^{2}\,C^{-1}}\)

**The LEFT face**, at \(x = -5\) cm. Its outward normal is \(-\hat{i}\), and there \(\vec{E} = -100\,\hat{i}\):

\(\phi_L = \left(-100\,\hat{i}\right)\cdot\left(-A\,\hat{i}\right) = +100A = 4\pi \times 10^{-2}\ \mathrm{N\,m^{2}\,C^{-1}}\)

**Both flat faces give POSITIVE flux**, and that is the key observation. The two minus signs multiply to a plus: the field points outward at **both** ends, so flux leaves the cylinder at each. They **add** rather than cancel.

\(\phi_{\text{total}} = 4\pi \times 10^{-2} + 4\pi \times 10^{-2} = 8\pi \times 10^{-2}\)

\(\boxed{\ \phi = 25{\cdot}1 \times 10^{-2} \approx 0{\cdot}25\ \mathrm{N\,m^{2}\,C^{-1}}\ }\)

**(b) The net charge inside.**

By Gauss's theorem,

\(\phi = \dfrac{q}{\varepsilon_0} \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad q = \varepsilon_0\phi\)

\(q = \left(8{\cdot}85 \times 10^{-12}\right)\left(25{\cdot}1 \times 10^{-2}\right)\)

\(\boxed{\ q = 2{\cdot}2 \times 10^{-12}\ \mathrm{C} = 2{\cdot}2\ \mathrm{pC}\ }\)

**The positive charge is what the outward flux implies.** Field lines emerge from the enclosed region on both sides, which is the signature of a net positive charge sitting at the plane \(x = 0\).

**What the field description is really saying.** \(\vec{E}\) reverses direction across \(x = 0\) while keeping the same magnitude — a **discontinuity** at that plane, and a discontinuity in \(E\) is exactly what a sheet of charge produces. The field of an infinite sheet of surface density \(\sigma\) is \(\sigma/2\varepsilon_0\) on each side, pointing away; setting \(\sigma/2\varepsilon_0 = 100\) gives \(\sigma = 1{\cdot}77 \times 10^{-9}\ \mathrm{C\,m^{-2}}\), and multiplying by the cylinder's cross-section \(4\pi \times 10^{-4}\ \mathrm{m^{2}}\) returns \(2{\cdot}2\) pC \(\checkmark\).

**Why the LENGTH of the cylinder is irrelevant.** Only the flat faces contribute, and their flux depends on the field there — which is the same at any \(x \ne 0\), since \(\vec{E}\) is uniform on each side. A longer or shorter cylinder would enclose exactly the same patch of the charged plane, and so the same charge.

rows.chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
rows.subtopic: Einstein's Photoelectric Equation and the Photon
rows.stem:
Answer the following, giving reasons :
(a) The maximum kinetic energy of the photoelectrons is independent of the intensity of incident radiation.
(b) Photoelectric current increases with the increase in the intensity of the incident radiation.
(c) The stopping potential \(\mathrm{V_0}\) varies linearly with the frequency \(\nu\) of the incident radiation for a given photosensitive surface.
rows.solution:
**(a) Why \(K_{\max}\) does not depend on intensity.**

**Because intensity fixes the NUMBER of photons, not the energy of each.**

\(K_{\max} = h\nu - \phi_0\)

**A photon is absorbed entirely by a SINGLE electron** — all or nothing, and it cannot be shared. So the energy any one electron receives is \(h\nu\), fixed by the frequency alone. Doubling the intensity doubles how many such transactions occur each second, but every one of them still delivers exactly \(h\nu\).

**Since \(h\nu\) and \(\phi_0\) are both unchanged, \(K_{\max}\) is unchanged.** Nothing in the equation refers to intensity at all.

*The wave picture predicts the opposite,* and that is what makes this observation decisive: a more intense wave has a larger field amplitude and should shake electrons loose with **more** energy. It does not.

**(b) Why the photocurrent grows with intensity.**

**Because intensity IS the number of photons arriving per second.**

\(\text{intensity} \propto \text{photons per second}\)

Each photon above threshold can liberate **one** electron. So more photons per second means more photoelectrons per second, and the photocurrent — which is charge per second — rises in proportion.

\(\text{photocurrent} \propto \text{intensity}\)

**Note what does NOT change**: the electrons come off no faster, only in greater numbers. The stopping potential stays exactly where it was.

**(c) Why \(V_0\) varies linearly with \(\nu\).**

The stopping potential is defined by \(eV_0 = K_{\max}\), so Einstein's equation becomes

\(eV_0 = h\nu - \phi_0\)

**Dividing through by \(e\):**

\(\boxed{\ V_0 = \left(\dfrac{h}{e}\right)\nu - \dfrac{\phi_0}{e}\ }\)

**This is \(y = mx + c\)** with \(V_0\) as \(y\) and \(\nu\) as \(x\) — hence a **straight line**.

\(\text{slope} = \dfrac{h}{e}, \qquad \text{intercept on the } V_0 \text{ axis} = -\dfrac{\phi_0}{e}\)

*To draw it:* a straight line rising to the right, cutting the \(\nu\)-axis at the threshold \(\nu_0\) and the \(V_0\)-axis at a negative value.

**The slope contains NO property of the metal** — only \(h\) and \(e\), both universal. So **every** photosensitive surface gives a line of the **same gradient**; different metals give **parallel** lines, displaced along the frequency axis according to their work functions. That is the single most striking feature of the graph, and it is what let Millikan measure \(h\) from the photoelectric effect and find it in agreement with Planck's value from black-body radiation — two entirely unrelated experiments.

**How the three parts fit together.** (a) and (b) separate the two things light can do — deliver energy per photon, and deliver photons per second. **Frequency controls how energetic; intensity controls how many.** (c) is the quantitative statement of the first, and the linearity is the evidence that energy really does arrive in packets of \(h\nu\).

rows.stem:
Name the electromagnetic radiations and write their frequency range :
(a) Used to take the photograph of the bones
(b) Produced by hot bodies
(c) Used in television communication systems
rows.solution:
**(a) Used to photograph bones.**

\(\boxed{\ \text{X-RAYS}\ }\)

**Frequency range:** about \(10^{16}\) Hz to \(10^{20}\) Hz.

*Why they work for this.* X-ray photons carry thousands of electronvolts, enough to pass through soft tissue while being strongly absorbed by the calcium in bone — absorption rises steeply with atomic number. The shadow cast on the film is the image. Their wavelength, around \(10^{-10}\) m, is also comparable to atomic spacing, which is why the same radiation diffracts from crystals.

**(b) Produced by hot bodies.**

\(\boxed{\ \text{INFRARED RADIATION}\ }\)

**Frequency range:** about \(10^{12}\) Hz to \(10^{14}\) Hz.

*Why hot bodies emit here.* Every object radiates according to its temperature, and at ordinary temperatures the peak of that emission falls in the infrared — Wien's law puts a \(300\) K body's peak near \(10\ \mu\)m. Infrared photons carry about \(0{\cdot}01\) to \(1\) eV, which matches the **vibrational** energies of molecules, so infrared is both emitted and absorbed readily by warm matter. That is why it is felt as **heat**, and why thermal imaging works at night.

**(c) Used in television communication.**

\(\boxed{\ \text{RADIO WAVES}\ }\)

**Frequency range:** about \(10^{5}\) Hz to \(10^{9}\) Hz. *(Television broadcasting occupies the VHF and UHF bands within this, roughly \(50\) to \(900\) MHz.)*

*Why this band.* Radio waves are produced easily by accelerating charges in an aerial, they carry far, and — crucially for television — the **UHF** band passes through the ionosphere's lower layers and diffracts around obstacles well enough for ground-based reception, while being high enough in frequency to carry the wide bandwidth a picture needs.

**The single principle behind all three.** What a band is used for is decided by its **photon energy** \(E = h\nu\), and hence by what it can interact with:

| Band | Photon energy | What it couples to |
|---|---|---|
| Radio | \(\sim 10^{-9}\) to \(10^{-5}\) eV | bulk **currents** in an aerial |
| Infrared | \(\sim 0{\cdot}01\) to \(1\) eV | molecular **vibration** |
| X-ray | \(\sim 10^{2}\) to \(10^{5}\) eV | **inner-shell** electrons; ionisation |

**The ordering to keep.** Frequency rises radio → microwave → infrared → visible → ultraviolet → X-ray → gamma, and photon energy rises with it while wavelength falls. All three named here travel at the same speed \(c\) in vacuum and obey the same four Maxwell equations; only the frequency distinguishes them.

rows.subtopic: AC Voltage Applied to an Inductor and a Capacitor
rows.stem:
An ac source of voltage \(\mathrm{V} = \mathrm{V_0} \sin \omega t\) is connected to a circuit element X. It is observed that the current flowing through X varies as \(\mathrm{I} = \mathrm{I_0} \sin\left(\omega t - \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)\).
(a) Identify the element X and write the expression for its reactance.
(b) Plot a graph to show the variation of reactance of the element with the frequency of the applied voltage.
(c) Draw plots showing the variation of voltage and current with time over one cycle of applied ac.
rows.solution:
**(a) Identifying the element.**

Compare the two waveforms:

\(V = V_0\sin\omega t, \qquad I = I_0\sin\left(\omega t - \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)\)

**The current's phase is \(\pi/2\) BEHIND the voltage's** — the current **LAGS** by a quarter cycle.

\(\boxed{\ \text{X is an INDUCTOR}\ }\)

**Its reactance:**

\(\boxed{\ X_L = \omega L = 2\pi\nu L\ }\)

**How the sign of the phase identifies the element.** A **capacitor** would make the current **lead** by \(\pi/2\), giving \(I = I_0\sin\left(\omega t + \pi/2\right)\); a **resistor** would leave it in phase. The minus sign in the bracket is therefore the whole identification — and the mnemonic **CIVIL** captures it: in a **C**apacitor **I** comes before **V**, while **V** comes before **I** in an **L**.

**Why an inductor makes the current lag.** It opposes any **change** in current, so the current cannot respond instantly to the driving voltage and trails behind. Deriving it: with \(v = L\,di/dt = V_0\sin\omega t\), integrating gives \(i = -\left(V_0/\omega L\right)\cos\omega t\), which is \(\left(V_0/\omega L\right)\sin\left(\omega t - \pi/2\right)\) — the lag appears from the integration itself, and the quarter cycle is not a choice but a consequence.

**(b) Reactance against frequency.**

\(X_L = 2\pi L\,\nu\)

*To draw it:* plot \(X_L\) vertically against frequency \(\nu\) horizontally. Since \(L\) is a constant, this is \(y = mx\) — a **STRAIGHT LINE through the ORIGIN**, of slope \(2\pi L\).

**Two features to show.** It **passes through the origin**: at \(\nu = 0\) (direct current) the reactance is **zero**, so an ideal inductor is just a piece of wire to DC. And it **rises without limit**: at high frequency the inductor chokes the current off, which is why it is called a **choke**.

*Contrast with a capacitor*, whose \(X_C = 1/2\pi\nu C\) is a rectangular hyperbola — infinite at \(\nu = 0\) and falling towards zero. The two are complementary, which is what makes filters possible.

**(c) Voltage and current against time.**

*To draw it:* one set of axes, one full cycle from \(\omega t = 0\) to \(2\pi\).

**The voltage** \(V = V_0\sin\omega t\) starts at **zero**, rises to \(+V_0\) at \(\omega t = \pi/2\), returns to zero at \(\pi\), reaches \(-V_0\) at \(3\pi/2\), and closes at \(2\pi\).

**The current** \(I = I_0\sin\left(\omega t - \pi/2\right) = -I_0\cos\omega t\) starts at its **negative peak** \(-I_0\), crosses zero (rising) at \(\omega t = \pi/2\), peaks at \(+I_0\) at \(\pi\), and crosses zero again at \(3\pi/2\).

**The current curve is the voltage curve shifted RIGHT by a quarter period** — it reaches every feature a quarter cycle **after** the voltage does. Label the shift, since that is what the plot exists to show.

**What the graph reveals about power.** The two curves have **opposite signs for half of each cycle**, so the instantaneous power \(P = VI\) is negative through those intervals: the inductor is **returning** energy to the source. Over a complete cycle the positive and negative areas cancel exactly, and the average power is **zero** — consistent with the power factor \(\cos\phi = \cos 90^\circ = 0\).

**An ideal inductor therefore dissipates nothing.** It stores energy in its magnetic field for a quarter cycle and gives it all back in the next, which is why the current in a purely reactive branch is called a **wattless current**: real, sometimes large, and heating nothing.
